courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Projecting Gaussians to splats and sorting them by tile
md: The sort is per tile, by each Gaussian's center depth, not per pixel. Where two large splats interpenetrate, the true order can differ from pixel to pixel, so blending is approximate. The paper notes this error becomes negligible as splats shrink toward pixel size, and lists sudden order switches (popping) as a limitation.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
md: "Garbage collection solves ABA" is a common misconception that Michael calls out. GC prevents ABA caused by *reuse*, but if a program moves the same nodes back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a node can leave and return to the same position with perfect GC. Ask whether the algorithm is ABA-safe under GC first; only then do hazard pointers or epochs make it ABA-safe without GC.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Reporting an ablation people can trust
md: Report per-stage deltas with intervals, the paired test and effect size, win/loss counts, interaction cells for stages that depend on each other, and cost, all on one stated harness. A bare column of mean scores invites the wrong conclusion.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Mass assignment and property-level authorization
md: Field lists rot in one direction: new fields. A blocklist that forbids `isAdmin` today silently allows `isOwner` added next quarter. An allowlist forgets a new field by leaving it read-only, which fails safe.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM: challenge and response, and why the hash is enough
md: NTLM never sends the password, but its proof is computed only from the unsalted NT hash plus a server challenge. So the hash is the password. Move to NTLMv2 only, then to Kerberos, and watch 4776 and the 4624 package name.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: DCSync: asking a domain controller for every password
md: 4662 is only written if Directory Service Access auditing is on **and** the domain object's SACL asks for it. Many domains have neither, and then DCSync leaves no Security log trace at all. Check before you need it.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: The exploit lifecycle: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload
md: Exploitation is a ladder of capabilities: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload. Every mitigation removes or weakens one rung, and the earlier the rung, the more bug-specific and costly the attacker's workaround.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Red team, pentest, purple team: three different questions
md: Pentest: find and fix weaknesses in a scope. Red team: measure whether people, process and technology detect and respond to a realistic adversary. Purple team: improve detection together, technique by technique. Adversary emulation is the method underneath the last two: play a specific, intelligence-backed threat.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Case: CISA's red team at a critical infrastructure organisation
md: A red team report is most valuable when it records, for every step, what the defenders should have seen and did not. AA23-059A does this in both phases, which is why its findings turn directly into detections and hardening work.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: tau-bench: simulated users, database state and pass^k
md: pass@k rewards finding a solution in k tries (useful when a verifier can pick the winner). pass^k rewards solving it every time (what a deployed agent needs). For independent trials with success p they are $1-(1-p)^k$ and $p^k$; across tasks, pass^k depends heavily on how p is spread.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Why an agent cannot just replay its whole history
md: Misconception: a memory layer makes the agent remember *better* than full history. On LoCoMo, where a conversation still fits in the window, full context scored highest in the Mem0 paper. Memory wins when history no longer fits, or when the cost and latency of re-reading it every turn are unacceptable.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Layer the checks: deterministic first, judges last
md: The multiplication assumes independent errors, which is optimistic. A judge and a test suite written from the same misunderstanding of the spec fail on the same wrong answers, so the real chain FPR is higher than the product.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: The map: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
md: LLM09 Misinformation is closer to reliability than to classic security, and other frameworks would not list it. It still lands companies in court (lesson 15), so engineers own it too.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Improper output handling: model output is untrusted input
md: "The model wrote it, so it's ours" is the mistake. Output is shaped by every token in the context, including retrieved pages and emails. Validate it exactly as strictly as you would a form field from an anonymous user.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Testing it: red teaming, benchmarks and AI for defenders
md: Measure both utility and attack success, test with adaptive and varied attacks, and prefer defences whose success does not depend on recognising the attack's wording.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: The soft watermark: add delta to the green logits
md: $\delta$ trades watermark strength against quality; $\gamma$ sets how often human text hits green by chance. The detector depends only on $\gamma$ and the hash rule, never on $\delta$, so a provider can change $\delta$ per product without changing the detector.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Replaying workloads to compare allocators
md: Workflow: capture once with an interposer, analyze with a heap profiler to find what to fix in code, convert to a workload, then replay that one workload against each allocator or tuning and compare RSS against ideal RSS.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Anomalies in time: seasonal baselines and robust residuals
md: For time series, first remove what is predictable (seasonality and level), then apply a robust score to the residual. The detector is only as good as the baseline: a residual is anomalous relative to a model of normal for that moment.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OAuth 2.0: delegated access without sharing a password
md: OAuth is about **authorization**: letting a client act on a user's behalf with limited scope. The access token is meant for the resource server, not for the client to learn who the user is. Logging users in needs OpenID Connect (lesson 10).

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Validating a JWT correctly: algorithm, signature, iss, aud, exp, nbf
md: Misconception: "we validate the token at the API gateway, so services can just decode it." Then any path around the gateway, and any token for another audience the gateway also accepts, reaches services that trust it blindly. Each service should at least check the audience meant for it.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: What an application security programme is, and who owns what
md: "Security owns security" is the most common misconception. A central team that tries to fix everything becomes a bottleneck and then gets bypassed. The working model: developers own fixes, the security team owns the system that makes fixes happen.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Testing the running app: DAST, IAST, SCA recall and fuzzing in CI
md: No method sees everything. SAST and SCA see code and dependencies early; DAST sees the deployed surface; IAST sees runtime paths the tests exercise; fuzzing sees parsers under abuse. Pick by what your application does: an API with a heavy parser needs fuzzing more than a static brochure site does.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Metrics that matter: time to remediate, open age and coverage
md: Measure what is still open and what you cannot see. Mean time to remediate, open age, SLA compliance and coverage together describe a programme; any one alone can be gamed by accident.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Why a question is not a short version of its answer
md: Misconception: *a text's embedding is a fixed property of the text.* In a role-aware model the same string gets one vector as a query and a different vector as a document, by design. Which vector you get depends on how you called the model.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Rate limits as token buckets: RPM, token limits and headers
md: Do not cache or replay a 429 as if it were an answer. RFC 6585 says responses with status 429 "MUST NOT be stored by a cache". Also note that a 429 is not always temporary: Anthropic returns 429 without a `retry-after` header when an organization reaches its monthly spend cap, and retrying keeps failing until access resumes.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
md: `volatile` does not fix this. In C and C++ it stops the compiler from removing or reordering accesses within one thread, which suits signal handlers and memory-mapped I/O, but cppreference states it is not suitable for communication between threads. A volatile `counter++` is still a separate read and write.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
md: Mean pooling suits sounds that last (rain, engine hum, music) and resists one-patch glitches. Max pooling catches short events (a bark, a door slam, a gunshot) but turns any single false patch into a clip-level false alarm. PANNs combines both inside the network: its global pooling sums the time-averaged and the time-maximized feature vectors.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Slow on purpose: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id and cost parameters
md: Store passwords with Argon2id (or scrypt, or bcrypt for legacy), a unique salt per user, and a cost tuned as high as your login traffic allows. Record the parameters with each hash, and raise them over time.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Passkeys and WebAuthn: why phishing stops working
md: Passkeys resist phishing because the browser binds every signature to the real site's origin and the credential to the site's domain. The user's judgment is not part of the security argument.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: One API in front of many models: the Converse call
md: Converse unifies the **shape** of requests and responses, not the **behavior** of models. Models still differ in quality, context length, supported content types and tool support, which the docs list per model. A one-line modelId swap is easy; validating that the new model is good enough is still your job.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: BitLinear: a matrix multiply made of additions
md: "Matmul becomes additions" applies to the weight matrices. Attention scores (queries Q times keys K, then the attention weights times values V) multiply activations by activations, so they are not ternary. And the speedup only appears with a kernel that actually exploits ternary weights, which lesson 5 covers.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Branchless code: cmov, masks and lookup tables
md: `cmov` with a memory operand always reads memory, even when the condition is false (the Intel pseudocode does `temp := SRC` first and lists page faults as possible). So a compiler cannot turn `p ? *p : 0` into a cmov from `*p`: it would fault on a null pointer. C's `?:` only evaluates the chosen side; branchless code evaluates both.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost
md: Leveled: low space and read amplification, high write amplification. Tiered: low write amplification, more runs to read and up to about 2x temporary space during a full merge. The size ratio T slides each policy along its curve.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Resilience, continuity and recovery: the words and the plans
md: A disaster recovery plan is not a business continuity plan. The DRP brings systems back at another site; the BCP keeps the business working while they are gone, often by hand. Maersk staff booked containers through WhatsApp and personal Gmail during NotPetya: that was continuity without systems, improvised because it was not planned.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups nobody restored: monitoring and testing that prove recovery
md: A green backup dashboard measures jobs, not recovery. Measure what a restore needs: the latest *verified restorable* point (your real RPO) and the last measured restore time at full size (your real RTO). Restore time grows with data size, so a test on last year's volume says little about today's.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: When recovery tools fail too: CrowdStrike 2024, keys and break-glass
md: A recovery key stored only inside the thing it recovers is not a recovery key. The same goes for admin passwords in a vault that runs on the failed platform, runbooks on the wiki that is down, and an on-call rota in the chat tool that is offline.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive
md: Bytes remove the vocabulary and its blind spots, but multiply the number of positions by roughly 4. Since compute is about $2mT$, a byte model is only practical if the big network runs on far fewer positions than there are bytes.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit
md: Byte models trade a tokenizer for an extra design choice: how to group bytes. With learned, entropy-based patches, BLT matched BPE models at 8B for equal training FLOPs, improved robustness and spelling, and turned patch size into a knob that trades steps for model size.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
md: Audit unsafe code at the module boundary. Keep fields that unsafe code trusts private, check every invariant before the unsafe block (as `assert!(mid <= len)` does), and write a SAFETY comment that names the invariant.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
md: Arrange data so that what you use together sits together, and walk it in address order. Stride 1 is the cheapest pattern there is.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Pruning by influence and grouping supernodes
md: Influence is unsigned. A feature that strongly *inhibits* the answer scores as high as one that promotes it. Use influence to decide what to look at, then read the signed edges to decide what it does.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: EM can only separate rank from document if the same documents appear at different ranks, and those overlaps must link all ranks together. When ranker 2 was D, E, B, A, C instead, ranks {1, 4} and {2, 3, 5} never shared a document, the relative scale between the two groups was unidentifiable, and EM's answer for rank 2 depended on its starting point: 0.63 starting from 0.5, 0.53 starting from 0.3 (truth 0.5).

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stopping CSRF: SameSite, tokens, Origin and Fetch Metadata
md: Cross-site scripting defeats every CSRF defence, as the Samy worm showed by reading MySpace's token. CSRF defences assume the attacker is outside your origin. Fix XSS first; then CSRF defences mean something.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Where the evidence lives when there is no server to seize
md: Misconception: "the provider keeps everything, so we can ask for the logs after the incident". The provider keeps only what its defaults keep: for example CloudTrail's 90-day event history of management events. Data events, flow logs and many SaaS audit logs never exist unless you enabled them, and no support ticket can bring them back.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Containers, serverless and autoscaling: evidence that deletes itself
md: Misconception: "we can investigate the pod later". Restarts, deploys, evictions and autoscaling all destroy local evidence on their own schedule. Ship container logs and audit logs off the cluster continuously, and make "relabel and cordon, then capture" the first move, not "delete and redeploy".

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Resource control policies and the data perimeter
md: RCPs can break things you did not know depended on outside access: a partner's integration, a third-party monitoring tool, an AWS feature using a service principal. AWS "strongly recommends" not attaching RCPs to the root without testing; review IAM Access Analyzer's external access findings and CloudTrail AccessDenied errors first, then roll out OU by OU.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The cloud from a security view: computers you rent through an API
md: In the cloud every resource is managed through a public API, so whoever holds valid credentials can act from anywhere. The main walls are identities, permissions and configuration, not the office network.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Secrets and keys: KMS, envelope encryption and secret stores
md: Encryption at rest only protects you from people who cannot use the key. If the same over-broad role can both read the bucket and call Decrypt, as an application role often can, the encryption adds an audit trail but no barrier. Grant `kms:Decrypt` as narrowly as the data itself.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Gaussian mixtures and EM: soft k-means with a shape per cluster
md: BIC's promise is asymptotic: the scikit-learn guide says it recovers the true number of components "only in the asymptotic regime", with much data actually drawn from a Gaussian mixture. On small or lumpy data, single-point components can buy unlimited likelihood. Look at the fitted variances before trusting a BIC curve, and treat `reg_covar` as a statement about the smallest cluster you believe in.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: Arrow is not a file format for long-term storage like Parquet. Arrow data is laid out for fast random access and computation and is normally uncompressed in memory (the IPC format allows only optional LZ4 or ZSTD buffer compression); Parquet is encoded and compressed for small size on disk. A typical pipeline reads Parquet and decodes it into Arrow-style (or engine-specific) column vectors.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inside the optimizer: IR, SSA and the classic scalar passes
md: Compilers optimize an IR in SSA form: one definition per value, with phi nodes where paths merge. mem2reg takes variables out of memory; constant propagation, DCE and CSE simplify straight-line code; LICM and strength reduction slim loops; the back end selects instructions, allocates registers and schedules.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: PGO optimizes for the inputs you profiled. The Clang manual warns that code not exercised in the profile "will be optimized as if it is unimportant". Profiling only a unit-test suite or a single toy input can make the real workload slower.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Why long tasks fail: compounding errors and verification
md: Task success is roughly a product of step successes, so long tasks need both a high per-step rate and a check after each step that actually detects failure. Check the resulting state, not just whether an action ran.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
md: TSan only sees code paths that actually run (the manual: it cannot find races in code paths that are not executed). And if, in this particular run, the two threads happened to pass through some unrelated lock in between, that lock creates a happens-before edge and hides the race. Coverage and varied workloads still matter.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time
md: Linearizability is not serializability. Serializability is about transactions over many objects appearing in *some* serial order, with no real-time rule. Linearizability is about single operations on one object, *with* the real-time rule. Their combination is strict serializability.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Consistent hashing with bounded loads: a hard cap per server
md: The balance factor c is a dial between two goods: low c gives tight balance but forwards more requests away from their natural owner (more misses for caches); high c keeps affinity but tolerates more imbalance.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Arc consistency: AC-3 prunes domains before guessing
md: Search guesses; propagation deduces. Every modern CP solver alternates: make one decision, propagate to a fixpoint (repeat until no rule deletes anything more), and backtrack only when some domain becomes empty.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission
md: Misconception: "a signature means the image is safe". A signature proves who produced it and that it was not changed since. A signed image can still contain vulnerable packages or a backdoor that entered upstream, as in the xz-utils case from the Linux course. Combine signing with scanning and provenance.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
md: AWS states it plainly: "Containers are not a security boundary, and the use of IAM roles for service accounts does not change this." Workload identity scopes credentials per pod, but an escaped container can act as anything on the node. Also, pods with hostNetwork: true always reach IMDS.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Exposed dashboards, kubelets and Docker APIs
md: Exposed management APIs are the most common real container compromise, and the usual payoff is mining. Every API that can start or exec into containers must require authentication and sit off the internet.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state
md: Misconception: a good standalone rewrite makes state unnecessary. To handle *drop the salary limit*, the rewrite must restate every surviving constraint as text, and the search engine must parse those constraints back into filters. That is two lossy conversions per turn, and a deleted constraint can come back if either one slips.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: When to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing
md: Ask when the readings are close in probability and a wrong guess is costly or hard to notice. Otherwise, guess the most literal reading, act on it, and make the interpretation visible.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: A clean CoT is not evidence of safety for tasks that do not need a CoT. Chen et al. and Korbak et al. both warn that malign reasoning can happen in activations, so a monitoring-only safety case (an argument that a model is safe to deploy) fails there.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
md: The cost problem of cross-encoders is not mainly the quadratic attention. It is that the full model, linear layers included, runs for every pair at query time. A bi-encoder pays the same per-token cost too, but for the documents only once, offline.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Block ciphers: what AES actually does to 16 bytes
md: A block cipher on its own encrypts exactly one block. Real messages are many blocks, and how you chain them (the **mode**) decides whether patterns leak. Calling raw AES block by block is the mistake of the next lesson.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Every level of the hierarchy does the same thing: stage a tile in a faster, smaller memory and reuse it across as many math operations as the capacity of that memory allows. Tile shapes are the main tuning knobs of a CUTLASS GEMM.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: Fast CUTLASS kernels come from a few choices: tile shape (reuse versus occupancy and wave fit), stage count (latency hiding versus shared memory), kernel schedule (cooperative or ping-pong) and the epilogue fusion. CuTe layouts make each choice a type parameter instead of a rewrite.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
md: CXL makes memory placement a policy problem again. The hardware gives you a slower, bigger NUMA tier; the operating system (tiering) or the cluster manager (pooling) must keep hot data local and push only cold or untouched data to it.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
md: Under section 1 a failed attempt can be enough: the offence is about intent and knowledge, not success. 'I didn't get in' is not a defence to trying.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
md: "It's only code" is not an export defence. Sending exploit technology abroad can need a licence, and US rules also cover releasing controlled technology to foreign persons at home (a "deemed export", which the 2021 rule names). Disclosure to the people who will fix the bug is the carved-out case; selling capability is not.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
md: "Nobody asked me directly" is weak protection. Misprision is about *active concealment* of a known felony, and obstruction can be committed by causing others not to disclose. Changing records, drafting the NDA and signing statements you know mislead are acts, not silence.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Upweighting means repeating: epochs, data limits and domain weights
md: Epochs = weight x budget / unique tokens. Up to about 4 epochs repetition costs almost nothing; beyond that each pass is worth less, and by about 40 it is worthless. Cap epochs per domain and give the surplus to domains that still have unique data.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: Memory moves in cache lines. Lay out data so that the bytes a hot loop needs are packed together, and the bytes it skips live somewhere else.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark
md: Classify by the damage of disclosure (and of tampering or loss), not by how the data looks. Rate each information type, take the high-water mark for systems, and attach the result as a label that tools can read.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: How DLP recognises sensitive content
md: DLP is only as good as its detector's precision. Prefer labels and exact data match over generic patterns where you can; require context for high confidence; and measure precision on real traffic before turning on blocking. Hashed SSNs are not anonymous: with about a billion possible values, anyone holding the salt can hash them all, so guard the EDM hash file and salt as Restricted data.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test
md: Determinism is not one property. Pin the reduction order and you get run-to-run equality. Pin it independently of batch size and position and you get the property a server actually needs. Keep RNG state per request and you get reproducible sampling. Test each one with its own experiment, compare at the logit level, and either go bitwise or attach a measurement to your tolerance.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Least-privilege pipeline credentials: tokens, environments, secrets
md: GitHub's environment docs note that workflows on self-hosted runners are not run in an isolated container, even if they use environments. An environment controls when a secret is released, not what else on that machine can read it afterwards. Pair environments with clean runners (lesson 3).

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Training: a weighted average of masked-LM losses
md: Perplexities reported for diffusion LMs are usually upper bounds (written as a less-or-equal sign in the papers), not exact values. Comparing a bound to an autoregressive model's exact perplexity slightly favours the autoregressive model.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
md: Overlap hides latency, not bandwidth. If two prefill GPUs share that 25 Gb/s link and each finishes an 8K prompt every 1.45 s, they produce about 1.4 caches/s against a link that sustains about 1.5. Add a third and the link becomes the bottleneck, however well transfers overlap.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Carving: recovering files with no metadata at all
md: A carved file has no name, no path, no timestamps and no owner. You can testify that these bytes were on the disk at this offset. Who created them, and when, needs other evidence.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Why a billion vectors break in-memory graph indexes
md: Two numbers drive an SSD-resident index: **total reads per query** (limits throughput, since the SSD has a fixed IOPS budget) and **round trips per query** (limits latency, since each trip costs a few hundred microseconds). DiskANN attacks both: a graph with short search paths, and a search that issues several reads per round trip.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: KTO keeps DPO's implicit reward and reference model but drops pairing: each example is scored against a shared reference point (the estimated KL drift) instead of against a sibling answer. That lets it train on binary feedback, and on imbalanced data via $\lambda_D, \lambda_U$.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Scientist is for code that only reads. Its README says that because the candidate may or may not run, it is only safe for wrapping methods that do not change data. Write paths need different checks, such as comparing stored rows after the fact.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: The verifier: proving every path safe before it runs
md: The verifier runs once, at load time, and proves properties of **all** paths: bounded execution, typed pointers, null checks before dereference, initialized registers, in-bounds stack and map access. Because the proof is done up front, the JIT-compiled code needs no runtime checks and runs at native speed.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
md: An edge appliance combines the three things attackers want most: anyone can talk to it before logging in, it holds credentials with reach inside, and it is usually the least observed computer you own.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet
md: The service may need the internet; the admin interface does not. Put management on its own network or behind a separate enforcement point, and prove it with an outside scan.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
md: L1-Exact spends the requested budget even when the problem is easy, because its reward penalizes being too short. When the goal is a worst-case cost cap rather than an exact length, use the Max formulation, which matched or beat L1-Exact while often using up to 2x fewer tokens.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Worked configs: SwiftOnSecurity's sysmon-config and sysmon-modular
md: A Sysmon config is a written decision about what you will be able to investigate later. Read what your config excludes as carefully as what it includes, and keep it in version control like detection rules (logging-detection-engineering).

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
md: Real aggregates are not the clean sum of the appliances you know about. UK-DALE reports that in House 1, with monitors on almost every appliance, only 80% of the energy was sub-metered, partly because the 52 plug monitors themselves draw about 50 W. The $\varepsilon_t$ term is never zero.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes
md: Stripping is lossy. NFKC turns the superscript in `i⁹` into a plain `9`, and a stopword list (words deleted from every key because they seem uninformative) that drops `group`, `bank` or `the` can merge different companies. Strip only tokens that never distinguish entities in your data, apply cleaning to the matching key, and keep the original string.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: A tenant: the cloud directory behind every Microsoft 365 login
md: A tenant is a token issuer that many services trust. The questions that decide its security are: who can get a token, for which app, with which permissions, from where, and for how long.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Case: Midnight Blizzard inside Microsoft's own tenant (2024)
md: Midnight Blizzard turned one unprotected account into mailbox access through apps: find an app with power, create apps of your own, grant them an application permission. Defend by inventorying every tenant and app, enforcing MFA everywhere, and alerting on grants of high-risk application permissions.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Token theft and replay, and binding tokens to devices
md: Passkeys protect the login; device binding protects what the login produces. Use both, plus a compliant-device requirement, and keep revocation and CAE ready for the replay that gets through.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: The logs: sign-ins, audit, Graph activity and MailItemsAccessed
md: Sign-in logs say who got tokens, audit logs say what changed, Graph activity logs say what apps asked for, and MailItemsAccessed says which mail was touched. Export all four before you need them: default retention is 7 or 30 days.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
md: The maximum of many noisy scores is biased upward. Selecting a system on a query set uses up that set: its score for the winner is no longer an unbiased estimate. The bias grows with the number of systems tried (roughly like sqrt(ln N)) and shrinks with more queries (like 1/sqrt(n)).

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Contamination: when test queries leak into training data
md: Putting it together: split by query cluster and time, tune on dev, read a sealed and rotating test set rarely, report paired bootstrap CIs, correct for every comparison you run, and check for contamination with fresh queries the model could not have seen.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: What each mitigation does not stop, and where to practise
md: Combine layers so their blind spots do not line up: canary plus shadow stack or PAC for returns, CFI for forward edges, full RELRO for the GOT, PIE with high-entropy ASLR and no leaks, tagging or hardened allocators for the heap, and a sandbox around anything that parses untrusted input. Then keep fixing bugs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
md: A common misreading is that FedAvg averages the clients' answers. It averages their **parameters**. In this problem the sample-weighted average of the three local optima is 1.667 and the plain average is 2.0, while the true optimum is 2.3. Averaging models that have fully solved their own problems gives the wrong model.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
md: ACORN-$\gamma$ and ACORN-1 run the same search strategy, predicate subgraph traversal. They differ only in *where* the denser neighborhood comes from: stored at build time (ACORN-$\gamma$, faster search, slower build) or reconstructed from two-hop lookups at query time (ACORN-1, cheap build, somewhat slower search).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit
md: Misconception: "attention is two GEMMs, so it runs at GEMM speed." The softmax between them is cheap in FLOPs but runs on units hundreds of times slower than the tensor cores. FP8 makes it worse: matmul throughput doubles while exponential throughput stays the same.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Crossing lines and why the learned paths curve
md: Straight training targets do not mean straight sampling paths. Each conditional path is a line, but the marginal flow, which is what the network learns and what sampling follows, curves wherever many lines cross.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
md: Refinement says nothing about the steps the mapping hides. If the mapping ignores a variable that matters (say, durable state on disk), a wrong design can still refine the spec. Review the mapping as carefully as the spec.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: "FP8 training" does not mean every tensor is FP8. In the FP8 paper, DeepSeek-V3 and the NVFP4 report alike, only the *inputs* to GEMMs are FP8. GEMM outputs come out in BF16 or FP32, and normalizations, softmax, the master weights and optimizer state stay in higher precision. Lesson 4 shows what that means for memory and speed, and the recipes that push FP8 into communication and optimizer state too.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a fake quantizer for E4M3, MXFP4 and NVFP4
md: A fake quantizer reproduces a format's numerics, not its speed: what each value becomes after casting and scaling. Real hardware adds its own accumulation precision and order, so validate surprising results on the target GPU, but use the fake quantizer to test a recipe on your own tensors first.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: On macOS, Apple's Xcode clang ships without libFuzzer (the Atheris documentation says the same), and Homebrew's clang needs the SDK path (`-isysroot $(xcrun --show-sdk-path)`) to find system headers. On Linux, distribution clang packages include it.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: The Broadcom case was found by reverse engineering and code review, not fuzzing, and its lesson for fuzzers is about reach: the dangerous code ran only for specific frame types in specific connection states. A stateless fuzzer of single frames would rarely get there.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts
md: A distance counts edits (lower is closer). A similarity is a normalized score (higher is closer). The same raw distance means very different things for short and long strings, so either normalize or make the allowed number of edits depend on length.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
md: Geometric hashing moves the expensive work offline: every model is stored under every basis. At query time one correct scene basis is enough, and it never needs to know in advance which model point it corresponds to.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Geohash: interleave the bits, name the cell
md: A shared geohash prefix guarantees closeness: both points are inside the same cell. The reverse is false: two points can be meters apart and share no prefix, because they straddle a cell boundary. Every correct proximity search must look at neighboring cells, not just one prefix.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: A caching allocator turns slow, synchronizing driver calls into fast CPU-side bookkeeping. The price is that freed memory is *kept*, so reserved memory, not allocated memory, is what other processes on the GPU see.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
md: All of these allocators are the same pattern at different layers: grab big memory rarely, carve it with your own rules, and choose block sizes that match the workload. Equal sizes kill external fragmentation; growable virtual ranges kill slivers; stream order makes reuse cheap.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: These measurements come from older GPUs (Fermi and Kepler in the post, Volta in the guide). Absolute numbers on a current GPU will differ, and larger caches can hide some waste. The sector and bank rules they illustrate are the ones the current CUDA guides still document.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
md: Rank by gap times time share, with an attainable target instead of 100 percent. The biggest gap and the biggest win are usually different kernels, and a gap on a kernel with a small time share is never worth a rewrite.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
md: GraphRAG is not a better retriever for every question. For a specific fact ("Who supplies Rover X2 motors?") plain vector RAG already finds c2, and the paper itself shows vector RAG gives the most *direct* answers. GraphRAG's measured gains are on broad sensemaking questions, the ones that need an understanding of the whole corpus.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
md: Graph RAG variants differ in where they spend LLM calls: GraphRAG spends heavily at indexing (extraction, summaries, reports) and on map calls per global query; FastGraphRAG cuts extraction; LightRAG drops communities; HippoRAG drops summaries and lets PPR do the multi-hop work.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
md: A stop can appear twice in one trip, for example on a loop route where the bus starts and ends at the same stop. That is why `stop_sequence`, not `stop_id`, identifies a row of a trip. Code that keys stop times by `stop_id` alone silently overwrites one visit with the other.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
md: Without precise sampling, the "hot" instruction in `perf annotate` is often the one *after* the slow one, such as the instruction that consumes a load's result. Use `:pp` when you care about individual instructions.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Hardware supply chain, coordinated disclosure, and practice
md: Hardware security in one sentence: the hardware runs your program correctly, but not invisibly. Keep secrets out of shared state (constant-time code, isolation, separate secure processors), keep firmware and microcode current, measure what booted, and expect new variants.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
md: Huge pages are a trade: TLB reach and shorter walks against contiguity, alignment and memory overhead. Use a hugetlbfs pool when you need certainty, THP in madvise mode when the hot regions are known, and check the counters, because both mechanisms fall back silently.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Local, shared and parallel attention, and converting a Transformer
md: Choosing a layout: global attention layers buy exact recall at any distance for a growing KV cache; sliding windows cap the cache and cap exact recall with it; shared attention saves parameters, not cache; parallel heads keep a little attention, and a little KV, in every layer. Across these designs the published choices cluster around a small share of global attention, about 1 layer in 4 to 1 in 8, spread evenly.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: A common mistake is to treat a plant like an office network: run an aggressive vulnerability scan, push patches overnight, reboot to clean an infection. NIST warns that indiscriminate use of IT practices in OT 'may cause availability and timing disruptions'. In OT the security team works with control engineers, not around them.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How attacks on physical processes work
md: Three layers stood between the change and an overflow: humans watching the HMI (defeated by the replay), network monitoring (raised an alert at minute 10), and an independent safety system with its own sensor (tripped at minute 26). Design so that the last layer does not share any path with the first two.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Rules and maps: NERC CIP, IEC 62443, NIST, CISA and ATT&CK for ICS
md: Frameworks tell you what good looks like (62443, NIST), what is mandatory in your sector (NERC CIP for the bulk grid), and how attackers behave (ATT&CK for ICS). Use all three, but remember the cases: most real compromises came through remote access, default passwords and flat networks.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: OIDC as the modern alternative: the same job in JSON
md: SAML and OIDC answer the same questions: who issued this, about whom, for which app, for which login, until when, signed with which key. Learn the questions, and either protocol's fields become a checklist.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: The federation defender's checklist, and where to practise
md: Federation turns identity into a few keys and a trust list. Guard those like domain controllers, verify assertions with libraries that use only what was signed, keep sessions short and revocable, and join IdP and app logs so a login that the IdP never issued stands out.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: PAM vaults: check-out, rotation, and the Uber 2022 script
md: A PAM vault turns many secrets into one, rotates them after use, and ideally never shows them to people. That makes the vault and its administrators the most valuable target you own: protect them as the top of the control plane.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu always returns a threshold, even when nothing changed. On a pair with pure noise it will happily split the noise into two classes and flag a large fraction of the image. Check for a clear gap (or a minimum difference between class means) before trusting the mask.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Declaring, severity, the incident commander and the first hour
md: The IC decides and coordinates; they should not also be the person typing commands. When the IC is debugging, nobody is commanding.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Eradication and recovery: rebuild, credentials, krbtgt and backups
md: Replication is not backup. Synchronised copies (domain controllers, mirrored disks, cloud sync) receive the attacker's deletions and encryption as fast as your legitimate changes. Keep at least one copy offline and immutable, and practise restoring it.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Why escaping is fragile
md: Denylist filters ("block quotes, OR, UNION and --") are escaping's weaker cousin. They reject real input such as O'Brien, and they only stop the spellings someone thought of: SQL accepts comments, different case, different whitespace and many equivalent expressions. Lesson 9 shows a real product whose cleaning function was bypassed by finding a path where it was not applied.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Links, drains, timeouts and a CQ that never overflows
md: Size the **CQ** for the maximum number of completions that can be outstanding (including several per request for multishot operations, which post many completions from one request, lesson 5), not the SQ. Use `IORING_SETUP_CQSIZE` with `cq_entries`, and reap promptly.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: ReDoS: a regular expression that blocks every user
md: A backtracking regex is dangerous when one string can be matched in many ways: a quantifier inside a quantifier, alternatives that overlap such as `(a|a)*`, or several `.*` in a row. The slow case is the near miss, so a test with matching strings will never show it. On Node.js the cost is paid by every user of the process.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Finding and catching JavaScript bugs: tools, signals, practice
md: One idea runs through the whole course: in JavaScript the boundaries you assume (an object, a context, a module, a header, a renderer) are usually not security boundaries. Real boundaries are processes, operating system users, origins and authenticated messages. Put untrusted input and untrusted code behind one of those, and check permission where the data is used.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Checking linearizability: searching for a legal order
md: Linearizability checking is a search for one legal order inside the real-time constraints. Its cost is driven by how many operations overlap, so you control it by limiting operations per key and by turning known non-effects (like timed-out reads) into `:fail`.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: Three defences, in order: prune what cannot run, search within a budget you chose from a convergence curve, and promote only wins that are larger than the noise. A tuner without the third one is a random walk through your performance history.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: For memory-bound kernels, runtime is roughly bytes moved / bandwidth. Elementwise ops do so little math per byte that the only lever that matters is how many bytes cross the HBM boundary. Fusion cuts bytes, not FLOPs.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared
md: Soft gradient = (q - p) / T, which shrinks like 1 over T squared. Multiply the soft loss by T squared so temperature changes what is matched without changing how much it counts.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: A more accurate teacher is not automatically a better teacher, and a student that improves is not necessarily copying its teacher. Measure student accuracy directly; try a smaller or early-stopped teacher, or a teacher assistant, when the gap is large.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: Rounding error depends on the range of each group. Pre-RoPE keys, per-channel groups, sparse outliers and an FP16 first token all exist to keep group ranges narrow.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Reload or recompute: bytes versus prefill FLOPs
md: Compare bytes over bandwidth with FLOPs over throughput. Fast tiers (host DRAM, RDMA pools) beat prefill at almost any length; slow tiers only pay off for long prompts, big models, or a GPU that is busy anyway.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before
md: Lamport clocks do not detect concurrency. From $L(a) < L(b)$ you may conclude only that b did not happen before a. Any code that treats a larger Lamport timestamp as "definitely caused by" is wrong.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Searching millions of passages: candidates, centroids, PLAID
md: Cheap approximate scores filter, exact scores decide. PLAID is the same funnel as BM25 followed by a cross-encoder, built inside one model: centroid ids are the cheap representation and decompressed vectors are the precise one.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: BFS-like (breadth-first-search-like) is an interpretation from probing, not a built-in algorithm. Coconut was never trained to search, keeps no explicit visited set, and the parallelism narrows after a couple of thoughts.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Always handle the case where the search lands on the edge of the window. With stored min/max bounds, a hit on the boundary is the signal that a non-monotonic model may have pushed the true answer outside.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Why ranking needs its own loss function
md: Ranking metrics depend on the scores only through the **sort**. Learning to rank works around that either by optimizing a smooth stand-in loss (RankNet, ListNet) or, in LambdaRank and LambdaMART, by writing down the gradient we want directly. The coming lessons build each of these.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: The state is a key-value memory with room for about $d_k$ clean associations per head. Linear attention writes to it with a purely additive rule, so it can neither correct an old association nor make room for new ones.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Where things live: the Linux filesystem from a defender's view
md: Learn the map once: configuration in `/etc`, user secrets in `/home` and `/root`, shared scratch in `/tmp`, history in `/var/log`, the live view in `/proc`. Almost every later lesson points at one of these places.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening
md: Turning off password login does not help if an attacker can write to `authorized_keys`, and a private key copied from a laptop works from anywhere. Protect private keys with a passphrase, remove keys of people who leave, and review every `authorized_keys` file on your servers, including root's (`/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`).

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: CIS Benchmarks: what one recommendation contains
md: Applying Level 2, or even all of Level 1, to production without testing is how hardening projects cause outages. CIS itself recommends trying the guidance in a test environment first. A benchmark is a starting point that you tailor (next lessons), not a script to run blind.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Writing audit rules that answer real questions
md: `-w` watches are the older syntax; audit.rules(7) calls them deprecated and slower, recommending `-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -F path=... -F perm=wa` instead. Many published baselines still use `-w`, and both work. And remember the limit: audit sees system calls. Lesson 13 shows activity that never makes one.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Linux EDR and fleet telemetry: what sensors see and miss
md: Do not set kernel.io_uring_disabled fleet-wide without checking workloads: io_uring exists for performance, and some of your workloads may use it. This is a tailoring decision per host class (lesson 4).

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Immutable OS images: rebuild instead of repair
md: Immutable images make the OS read-only and replace it whole: drift and most persistence disappear, patching becomes shipping a tested image, and runtime telemetry focuses on the few writable areas. The price is new ways to debug and to run agents.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore, and where they fail
md: Overlap metrics measure closeness to a reference, not correctness. A fluent answer with one wrong fact can outscore a correct paraphrase. They also penalize outputs that are better than, but different from, the reference, which is common once a strong LLM writes the outputs.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Inside an inference server: one engine step at a time
md: The scheduler decides **what** runs each step, the KV cache manager decides whether it **fits**, and the executor just runs a forward pass over token ids and block tables. Almost every serving optimization in this course is a change to the first two.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Admission control is a bet about future output lengths. Reserve the worst case and you never preempt but waste memory; allocate on demand and you fit far more requests but need a preemption policy (latest arrival first, all of its blocks) and a recovery method (swap or recompute).

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Why hard constraints need filters, not similarity
md: The LLM never touches the documents. It only translates the query into a filter object. Exact enforcement is done by the search engine, which is cheap, deterministic and testable.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
md: Calls set the latency floor and the per-call overhead; tokens set the bill. Listwise minimizes calls, not tokens. PRP buys robustness to prompt order with 20 to 100 times more prompts than pointwise (220 to 1,100 times more than listwise) at k = 100.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
md: Both pointwise methods need token log-probabilities. Many chat APIs only return generated text, which is why the RankGPT authors could not run them on GPT-4. And because each passage is scored alone, the score must be comparable across passages (calibrated), which the PRP paper argues LLMs are not trained to provide.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: SIFT: keypoints across scale and a 128-number descriptor
md: A SIFT keypoint carries position, scale and orientation. The descriptor is computed in that local frame, which is why it survives zoom and rotation, and its 128 entries are L2-normalized and clipped for lighting robustness.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Treiber stack: one CAS on the top pointer
md: Pop reads `old->next` after loading `old` but before its CAS. If another thread pops `old` and frees it in that gap, the read touches freed memory. Worse, if the node is reused before the CAS, the CAS can still succeed with a stale `next`. That is the ABA problem, and it is the subject of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drain: a fixed-depth parse tree and a similarity threshold
md: The one thing to remember: Drain bounds the work per line to a fixed tree walk plus a comparison against the few groups in one leaf, which makes its cost $O(n)$ in the number of lines. It buys that speed with two assumptions, that same-template lines share a token count and that early tokens are constants.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Normalisation: one event, one shape (ECS and OCSF)
md: A Windows 4625 converted to ECS and an sshd failure converted to ECS look identical to a rule, which is the point, but also a risk: a mapping mistake (say, putting the target host into source.ip) now breaks every rule at once. Test mappings with sample events from each source, exactly like rules (lesson 11).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Baselines, anomalies and UEBA: how Storm-0558 was caught
md: State's advantage was not a product; it was three years of studying normal mailbox access, which let a modest-looking event stand out. The CSRB notes that buying the logs alone would not have been enough: few organisations analysed that voluminous log in detail.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
md: Ring Attention is not an approximation like sparse attention (each query sees only a chosen subset of keys) or sliding-window attention (each query sees only a fixed window of recent tokens). Each query still attends to every key; only the *order* and *location* of the work change. It also does not reduce FLOPs: total compute is the same quadratic amount, just spread over more chips.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
md: A loop is an algorithm's inner step. With enough iterations, a fixed-size block can resolve chains of references, simulate a small computer, or stand in for chain-of-thought steps, without adding parameters. How well *training* finds such a step is a separate, empirical question.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Learned depth per token: Mixture-of-Recursions, Ouro, HRM and TRM
md: Do not compare TRM's ARC numbers with LLM results as if they were the same kind of system. TRM is trained per task family on about 1000 augmented examples with a fixed answer grid; an LLM is a general text model. An independent ARC Prize analysis cited by the TRM paper found deep supervision drove most of HRM's gain (19% to 39%), while the two-level recursion added little (35.7% to 39.0%).

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: SISA is a training-time design decision. It cannot be retrofitted onto a model that was already trained on all the data, which is the situation for every existing LLM. That is why the rest of this course is about **approximate** unlearning: editing an existing model so it behaves *as if* it had been retrained, without a guarantee.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: Do not trust the malware's own story. A ransom note, a file name or an icon is chosen by the author. Classify by what the code actually does: NotPetya's note said ransomware, its code said wiper.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Dynamic analysis: sandboxes, monitors and the WannaCry kill switch
md: Never register or contact infrastructure from a live sample without authorisation and coordination. Hutchins' registration worked out, but researchers who touch attacker infrastructure can disrupt investigations or alert attackers. In your lab, the internet is fake by design.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Matryoshka training puts the most useful information in the first coordinates, so a prefix of the vector is a good small embedding. Without it, keeping the first m numbers of a normal embedding throws away information almost at random.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
md: Bubble = (p - 1) / (v m). 1F1B bounds activation memory to p microbatches; interleaving divides the bubble by v at the cost of v times more pipeline sends.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: An image is not a photograph: smear, footprint and checks
md: Treat a memory image as many snapshots stitched together. A single odd pointer or timestamp may be smear; a finding that two independent methods agree on is evidence.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics against memory analysis, and the cross-view answer
md: Every hiding trick must leave the hidden thing working, and working things touch the kernel: they have threads, memory, handles and sockets. Look for the part the attacker could not change without breaking their own code.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Measuring and fixing fragmentation in production
md: Fix the layer the numbers point at. Slack inside pages (active over allocated) needs objects moved or lifetimes grouped. Unused resident pages (resident over active) need purging or decay. Missing high-order physical blocks need compaction. Reaching for the wrong tool spends CPU and changes nothing.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
md: Removing a node and freeing it are different events. Every scheme in this course defers the free until no thread can still hold a reference taken before the removal.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
md: C and C++ do not check bounds or lifetimes for you. Every array index, every length and every `free` is a promise the programmer must keep by hand. Memory safety bugs are what happens when one promise is broken, and the attacker gets to choose the input.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Uninitialized memory and type confusion
md: Uninitialized reads leak what came before; type confusion reinterprets what is there. Both are fixed the same way in spirit: never let code read bytes whose meaning it has not established, by initializing first and checking tags before use.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: ArcFace: putting an angular margin inside a classifier
md: The class weights only cover training identities. At test time you discard them and compare normalized features with cosine similarity, exactly as with a triplet-trained model. A large classification accuracy on training classes is not the goal.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
md: Noise you can see and average away; bias you cannot. Vary the setup (layout, link order, process, machine) and trust only effects that survive the variation.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Bitwise-equal logprobs do not make an async run on-policy. True-on-policy alignment removes numerical mismatch between engines, not staleness from training on groups generated under older weights; the data buffer bounds that separately.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The attacker holds the phone: OWASP MAS and its threat model
md: Treat everything inside the app as readable and changeable by its user. The app's job is to protect the user's data from *other* parties (other apps, thieves, the network). Decisions about what a user is allowed to do belong on the server.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: WebViews: a browser inside the app, with a bridge to native code
md: A WebView bridge turns 'which page is loaded' into 'who can call our native code'. Control both: what may load, and which origin each bridge call came from.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Absorbing the up-projections: attend in latent space
md: Absorption is just regrouping a product of matrices: $q^{\top}(W c) = (W^{\top} q)^{\top} c$. It turns MLA decoding into MQA-shaped work over the latent cache, so no per-head key or value is ever stored or rebuilt.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Merge when one adapter dominates the traffic and per-token latency matters most. Keep adapters unmerged when many adapters are active concurrently, so the base matmul can be batched across all of them.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Asking for diversity cuts both ways. Raudaschl's repo has a diverse mode whose prompt asks for synonyms, broader or narrower framings and related sub-topics, and to avoid minor rewordings. That reduces redundancy but pushes phrasings toward the edge of the topic, where drift lives. Inspect generated queries on real traffic before tuning N.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Multi-token prediction keeps the input and the causal context the same and only adds targets: each position is asked for tokens t+1 through t+n, all from the prefix ending at t.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why orthogonalize: steepest descent under the spectral norm
md: This argument explains the *direction* of a single step, with moving averages switched off. It says nothing about momentum: Bernstein and Newhouse treat the averages as smoothing against mini-batch noise, and call their exact role an open question. Muon adds momentum for empirical reasons.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
md: An optimizer claim is only as good as its baseline. Ask: was the baseline tuned as hard, at more than one scale and data ratio, compared at the end of training, and in which unit (steps, tokens, FLOPs or hours)? Independent tests put matrix optimizers ahead of AdamW, by less than first reported.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Deriving the rules from one condition, and muP by hand
md: One rule generates muP: every weight and every update should have spectral norm about the square root of fan_out over fan_in. For Adam that means learning rate 1/fan_in for every layer; for SGD, fan_out/fan_in.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: Atomic does not mean cheap. An atomic write to a line that other cores are reading forces cache-line transfers, and in Bos's measurement it made another core's plain loads about 10 times slower on an older x86-64 machine.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC trades space for concurrency: every update leaves an old version behind so that readers already in flight can keep a consistent view without blocking writers.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
md: MVCC moves the cost of concurrency into the storage engine: dead versions to clean, index entries to maintain, and XIDs to freeze. Long-lived snapshots make all three worse.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
md: The gates are independent sigmoids, not a softmax. They do not have to sum to 1, so the model can turn several branches up or down at once. Also note what NSA does *not* do: it keeps the full KV cache (and three branches with independent keys and values), so it cuts the bytes *read* per step, not the bytes *stored*.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
md: MIH is fast only when substring buckets stay small. Norouzi et al. analyze uniformly distributed codes and find a substring length of about log2 of the database size works well. Highly skewed hashes (many near-blank images with the same hash) create giant buckets. PDQ's quality score, a 0 to 100 measure of how much detail an image has (next lesson), flags such featureless images so they can be filtered out.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: ARP spoofing up close, and how switches stop it
md: Static ARP entries on every laptop are not a practical fix: they break when hardware changes and do not scale. Put the check in the switch (DHCP snooping plus DAI), where one configuration covers every port, and encrypt traffic so a successful poisoner learns little.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Firewalls: stateless, stateful and application-aware
md: A firewall that allows port 443 allows every attack that arrives over port 443. Firewalls decide who may talk to whom on which port; whether the conversation itself is malicious is the job of the application, TLS, and IDS or application-layer inspection.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Suricata in depth: how rules match, EVE output and tuning
md: Every Suricata alert should send you to the flow behind it: pull the EVE records with the same flow_id (or the Zeek logs with the same Community ID) and decide from the full conversation, not from the alert message alone.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Network forensics for incident response: a worked IcedID investigation
md: Network forensics is pivoting with discipline: logs to scope, packets to prove, one UTC timeline, every step recorded. The attacker controls the infected host; they rarely control your sensor.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: UDP and ICMP: no handshake, and messages about the network
md: "Block all ICMP" is a common overreaction. It hides hosts from ping sweeps, but it also breaks useful signals such as fragmentation needed (type 3, code 4), which hosts rely on to size their packets. Filter selectively: allow the error messages your network needs, rate-limit echo, and log the rest.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Setting a policy does not move pages that already exist. `mbind(2)` affects only new allocations unless you pass the flag `MPOL_MF_MOVE` (or `MPOL_MF_MOVE_ALL`, which also moves pages that other processes share, and so needs CAP_SYS_NICE, a Linux capability: one of the slices of root privilege a process can hold). Install the policy before the first touch, or ask for migration explicitly.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
md: NVMe queue depth does not make flash faster; it lets the controller keep many dies busy. One synchronous 4 KB read at a time pays the full read latency per request no matter how many queues the drive has. Use async I/O (io_uring, the Linux asynchronous I/O interface built on shared submission and completion rings; SPDK, or many threads) to keep enough requests in flight.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
